passages.title: A Love Story in Five Chapters
passages.text:
Linh's first **date** with Nam was nothing special. He wanted to **take someone to** a fancy restaurant, but he chose a small noodle shop because he could not afford anything else. Still, they talked for hours, and Linh liked the way he laughed at himself.

After **a couple of weeks** they began to **go out with** each other regularly, and over the next months they started to **get to know** each other's families. Nam's mother was strict, but Linh managed to **get on with** her, which made everything easier. Several of Linh's friends had been **in love** before and had to **break up**, so she was careful, but this time she felt sure.

**The following year**, Nam asked her to **get engaged to** him on a mountain top at sunrise. The **ceremony** was held in her grandmother's village, and the **reception** that followed lasted until midnight. They chose to **go on honeymoon** in Nha Trang, and within a year Linh was lucky enough to **get pregnant**. Every **anniversary**, the couple return to the little noodle shop where it all began. Not every story ends so happily: Linh's cousin **got divorced** after only three years, because the two of them never learned to talk about their problems.

passages.title: Getting Ready for the Big Celebration
passages.text:
Hana's sister was graduating, and the whole family was invited to a big **celebration** at a hotel. Hana tried to **get dressed** quickly, but nothing went smoothly. First she discovered that she must **have got coffee on** her white blouse, so she chose a blue shirt instead. Then a **button** came off, the **zip** of her skirt got stuck, and one **sleeve** turned out to be shorter than the other because the shirt belonged to her cousin.

Finally, she added the finishing touches: a silk **scarf** around her neck, a thin silver **necklace**, a **bracelet** that her grandmother had given her, and a small **earring** in each ear. She checked her **collar** in the mirror and put her phone in her **pocket**.

Her mother smiled and said that she looked lovely, and her sister looked wonderful **as well**. **Afterwards**, everyone went out to the garden to take photos, and Hana forgot all about the small disasters of the morning.

passages.title: The Hiking Trip That Went Wrong
passages.text:
Last spring I decided to hike in the mountains **on my own**, because I wanted to enjoy the quiet **scenery** without any distractions. On the second day, however, things began to **go wrong**. The guide at the hostel had warned me that it is easy to **be injured** on wet rocks, but I ignored him, slipped and fell about three metres. When the rescue team found me, I was lucky to be **alive**.

At the hospital the doctors checked my **bladder** and **rectum** to make sure there were no internal injuries, and fortunately there were none. A dull pain continued to **linger** in my back for weeks, though, and I could not work.

The hospital bill was high, but years earlier my father had taught me to **put money away for a rainy day**. I had kept my savings in a **financial institution** **for a period of time**, and the bank agreed to **pay interest on** them, so I had enough. During my recovery, friends used to **come around** every evening with food and jokes. As soon as the doctor allowed it, I tried to **get on with** my work, a little wiser and much more careful.

passages.title: Choosing a Career and Learning English
passages.text:
In many countries, secondary students can be assessed **in up to ten subjects**, so choosing a career is not easy. Some prefer **vocational training**, which prepares them quickly for a job, while others go to university to study **engineering** and become **an engineer**, or choose **architecture** in order to become **an architect**. Students who are interested in people may pick **psychology** and hope to work as **a psychologist**. A few ambitious ones decide to **go into business** straight after school.

Whatever the choice, English helps. Mai, who wants to study abroad, has decided to **work on** her speaking every day. She knows it is not enough to **have a wide vocabulary**; she wants to speak both **accurately** and **fluently**. At first she used to **get things wrong** all the time, and she used to **have problems with** grammar and tenses. Now she tries to **pick things up** from films and podcasts, **in particular** from interviews with scientists.

Her teacher says she will **become more fluent** if she speaks every day, and that it matters little whether a student will **have a good accent** or not, as long as people can understand them clearly.
